deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Euler's practical application of his pipe-friction theory to fountains fed from an elevated reservoir (castellum). The setting is a reservoir raised a height q above the fountain orifice DD and joined to it by a pipe. With n = length/diameter, Euler has derived (previous pages) that the jet height is v = N(n)·q − M(n). Here N < 1 is a multiplicative loss factor. M is a subtractive height, in feet, that tends to 30 ft for large n; for n > 50000 the table gives N ≈ 4000/n and M = 30.

§114 (end): M comes from the atmospheric pressure. In Euler's friction law the friction depends on the absolute pressure, so M would scale in proportion if the atmosphere were heavier or lighter.

§115: no outflow occurs unless Nq > M, i.e. q > M/N. Example: n = 100000 gives N = 0.04 and M = 30, so q > 3000/4 = 750 ft. Conversely, for given q, the condition M/N < q fixes an upper limit for n, because M/N increases with n.

§116: a design rule for a given reservoir site and fountain site. Lay the pipe as straight as possible (minimal length) and make its bore as wide as circumstances allow, since the jet height depends chiefly on the diameter.

§117: worked example with q = 130 ft and b = 2500 ft, for diameters 1, 1/2, ..., 1/6 ft (n = 2500 to 15000). Euler tabulates N, M and v = 130N − M, obtaining 82.71, 52.80, 33.29, 20.19, 11.19 and 4.56 ft. The following page draws the conclusion that a diameter below about 1/7 ft gives no jet at all.
errors: Physical (not arithmetical) error: the theory makes friction depend on absolute pressure, Coulomb-like, so the atmosphere produces a finite threshold head and the subtractive term M. For water in pipes this is wrong: losses depend on velocity (Chézy/Darcy-type laws), not on absolute pressure, and there is no static threshold below which flow stops. This flawed character of E260 is known in the historical literature (e.g. Truesdell's account of Euler's hydraulics).

ideas.what: Threshold condition for any outflow, q > M/N, i.e. a minimum driving head below which friction stops the flow entirely
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb-type (static) friction threshold; formally analogous to a yield-stress (Bingham) threshold, though not intended as such
ideas.usually_credited_to: Coulomb friction ideas (Amontons, Coulomb); yield-stress fluids (Bingham 1916)

ideas.what: Jet height under pipe friction, v = Nq − M, tabulated against pipe diameter for a fixed reservoir height and distance
ideas.modern_name: Head-loss computation for a gravity-fed fountain or aqueduct
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hydraulic engineers (Couplet, Bossut, Chézy, Prony, Darcy-Weisbach)

ideas.what: Design rule: shortest (straight) pipe and largest feasible diameter maximize jet height
ideas.modern_name: Minimizing friction head loss in pipe design

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine numerical applications of Euler's known, and physically incorrect, pressure-dependent friction law. Only a minor arithmetic slip (11.19 for 11.15) is new; nothing appears unexploited or uncredited.
transcription_corrections: The inequalities in §115 are printed with a combined ≥/≤-style symbol (q ≥ 3000/4, M/N ≤ q) rather than strict > and <; this is minor.
In the table, the printed v for diameter 1/5 is 11,19 (faithfully transcribed), although the correct value is about 11,15.
